final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. Yes, but the paths differ. (1) The in absentia removal order should be attacked first, by a motion to reopen to rescind it filed with the immigration court (the Immigration Judge who entered the order) under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), on the ground of lack of notice. (2) The USCIS denials are separate: the I-130 and I-485 denials are USCIS actions, and the usual deadline to move USCIS to reopen or reconsider (Form I-290B) is 30 days (33 if mailed) from the decision, which expired long ago. The realistic routes are (a) rescind the order, then renew adjustment before the IJ, or (b) a new I-130 / request that USCIS reopen on its own motion because of its own mailing error.

A. IMMIGRATION COURT: WHAT TO FILE. File a motion to reopen to rescind the in absentia order and for a stay, with the immigration court that holds the record. Ground: the husband did not receive notice in accordance with INA 239(a)(1) or (a)(2). Such a motion may be filed at any time (no 180-day limit) and, under 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii), filing it automatically stays removal pending the IJ's decision. Only one such motion is allowed. Practical contents: motion with proposed order, cover page, the husband's sworn declaration (never lived at / never gave the address, never received the NTA or hearing notice, learned of the order on April 1, 2026), proof of his actual address (lease, bills, the I-130/I-485 forms showing the address he gave USCIS), evidence that USCIS used an address he never provided (the RFE and denial notices, the I-485 receipt), a copy of the order and the NTA/notice if available, and an EOIR-33 change of address. An attorney should file EOIR-28 with it. File through ECAS (electronic filing) or by mail, with proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA. If he is also eligible, plead in the alternative that the failure to appear resulted from exceptional circumstances; but that ground has a 180-day limit from the order (August 1, 2025 + 180 days = about January 28, 2026), so it is expired as of April 1, 2026, and the lack-of-notice ground is the only viable one. Request that the court also set the case for a hearing, and attach a copy of the adjustment application and I-130 evidence as the relief to be pursued (a motion to reopen should be accompanied by the application for relief sought).

Merits point on notice: Under INA 239(a)(1)(F) the NTA must be sent to the address the noncitizen provided; mail to an address he never provided is not notice under 239(a)(1) and cannot support in absentia under 240(b)(5)(A) (written notice must be given under 239(a)(1) or (2)). Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), holds that for in absentia purposes DHS need not give a single compliant NTA, and a later notice of hearing can satisfy 239(a)(2) for the specific hearing; but the husband's position is that no notice of any kind reached him or was sent to an address he provided, so the removal order cannot stand. Risks: if any hearing notice actually went to a correct address or he had a duty to keep address current (INA 239(a)(1)(F), 8 U.S.C. 1229(a)(1)(F)), the IJ may find notice sufficient; his I-485 pending in the USCIS address system is evidence that he did provide a proper address. Note: the 'address' facts must be proven by evidence; DHS's mailing to an incorrect address is the central fact.

B. FEES. As of April 1, 2026, no EOIR filing fee is required for a motion to reopen an in absentia order filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (lack of notice or custody): the statute creating the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) EOIR fees excludes it, and 8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2) exempts it. By contrast, other motions to reopen/reconsider before an IJ now carry an inflation-adjusted OBBBA fee of $1,045 for FY2026 (inclusive of the $900 base fee); this does not apply to the lack-of-notice motion. If the motion is granted and the case proceeds, later filings carry their own fees: the IJ-level adjustment application is filed with USCIS-type fee exposure (I-485 fee is paid to USCIS, not the court; renewed adjustment before the IJ has no separate EOIR fee but biometrics/ fees may apply), and the EOIR-42B/EOIR-26 fees are not relevant here. Any new OBBBA fee schedules effective October 1, 2026 postdate the April 1, 2026 answer date.

C. THE I-130 AND I-485. (1) USCIS: the I-130 was denied for abandonment/failure to respond to an RFE mailed to an address the couple never gave. A motion to reopen or reconsider (Form I-290B) must be filed within 30 days (33 if mailed) of the decision, 8 CFR 103.5(a)(1)(i), and no appeal lies from the I-485 denial (8 CFR 245.2(a)(5)(ii)); the I-130 denial for abandonment is also not appealable to the BIA (8 CFR 103.2(b)(15)). USCIS may reopen on its own motion (8 CFR 103.5(a)(5)(i)) and can excuse late filing only for motions to reopen where delay was reasonable and beyond control (103.5(a)(1)(i)), so a late I-290B showing USCIS's own mailing error is possible but discretionary. (2) Better path: once the removal order is rescinded and proceedings are reopened, the IJ has exclusive jurisdiction over adjustment for a noncitizen in proceedings (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1)), so the husband can renew the I-485 before the IJ; because the I-130 stands denied, the wife should file a new I-130 (with a new filing fee) and the IJ can adjudicate it, or USCIS may be asked to adjudicate the I-130 as a prima facie approvable petition (Matter of Hashmi factors for a continuance). A new I-130 does not need the first one to be reopened. Federal court review is a remote option (APA action against USCIS) and generally unavailable for discretionary adjustment denials.

D. SUBSTANTIVE RISKS. Adjustment under INA 245(a) as an immediate relative of a U.S. citizen does not require maintaining status (245(c) bars do not apply to immediate relatives), and overstay of the I-94 does not bar him. But he entered on a B-2 visa on December 1, 2022 and married 19 days later; the State Department 90-day rule creates a presumption of willful misrepresentation (preconceived intent) under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i) which could bar adjustment absent a waiver (INA 212(i) waiver via I-601 based on extreme hardship to the citizen spouse). This must be assessed before going back into proceedings. Also a bona fide marriage must be proven (INA 204(c) not apparent on these facts). Finally, if the order is not rescinded, he remains subject to removal (the automatic stay lasts only while the motion is pending; denial ends it, and a petition for review lies to the court of appeals within 30 days).

UNRESOLVED. I could not fetch eCFR, Federal Register, or the statute text directly (egress blocked), so exact regulatory language and the 8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2) subsection number come from search summaries and my background knowledge and are marked unverified; the specific USCIS regulations in part C (103.5, 103.2(b)(15), 245.2(a)(5)(ii), 1245.2) and Hashmi are from general knowledge, not fetched. Consult counsel and verify before filing.

issues.text: Jurisdiction/forum: immigration court (IJ) for in absentia order vs USCIS for I-130/I-485 denials
Motion to reopen to rescind in absentia order for lack of notice (no time limit, automatic stay, one motion)
Adequacy of notice: NTA/hearing notice mailed to address never provided; Campos-Chaves effect
EOIR filing fee for the motion as of April 1, 2026 (OBBBA fee exemption)
Recourse for USCIS denials: I-290B deadline, sua sponte reopening, new I-130, renewal of I-485 before IJ
Substantive eligibility risk: B-2 entry, marriage within 90 days, misrepresentation/preconceived intent

authorities.title: Rescission of in absentia order
authorities.proposition: In absentia order may be rescinded on motion filed at any time if alien did not receive notice under 239(a)(1) or (2); 180 days for exceptional circumstances; filing stays removal.

authorities.title: Reopening before the immigration court: in absentia
authorities.proposition: One motion to rescind in absentia order; lack-of-notice motion may be filed any time; automatic stay of removal pending IJ decision.

authorities.title: Campos-Chaves v. Garland
authorities.proposition: For in absentia rescission, notice of hearing under 239(a)(2) can suffice; a defective NTA alone does not guarantee rescission; must show no compliant notice for missed hearing.

claims.text: The husband may file a motion to reopen to rescind the in absentia order with the immigration court on lack-of-notice grounds at any time, which automatically stays removal.
As of April 1, 2026, no EOIR fee applies to a motion to reopen filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii).
Campos-Chaves limits reliance on a defective NTA alone; he must show no compliant notice of the hearing was received/sent to a provided address.
USCIS I-290B deadline is 30/33 days and has lapsed; practical recourse is renewing adjustment before the IJ with a new I-130 or requesting discretionary reopening.
